candidate.title: Brushing Scam with QR Code Twist
candidate.summary: Scammers ship unordered packages to your address using your name and a real tracking number so they can post fake "verified buyer" reviews, and increasingly tuck in a QR code that claims to help you find the sender or return the item but actually leads to a phishing or malware site.
safetyTips: Do not scan any QR code included inside an unexpected package; legitimate senders don't require this
Know that by law you are not obligated to return or pay for items you never ordered and can keep them as a gift
Change passwords on your online shopping and marketplace accounts if you scanned a code or suspect your information was compromised, and monitor your credit report at AnnualCreditReport.com
If the package came from Amazon or another marketplace, report it to the platform so they can investigate and remove the seller
Check your online marketplace accounts for reviews you didn't write and report any fraudulent ones
candidate.howItWorks: A stranger's package shows up on your doorstep addressed to you, often with no company name or a strange, unfamiliar business name and no real return address. A third-party online seller has obtained your name and address (often through a data breach) and shipped you a low-cost item so the delivery generates a legitimate tracking number and "verified purchase" status. The seller then uses your identity to post a glowing fake review, boosting their ratings on the marketplace. In a newer twist, the package includes a note with a QR code telling you to "scan to find out who sent it" or "scan for return instructions." Scanning takes victims to a phishing website designed to harvest credit card numbers, usernames, and passwords, or can install malware that gives hackers access to the device.
redFlags: An unexpected package arrives that you never ordered, often with no sender name or an unfamiliar, oddly-named company on the label
The package has no return address, or the return address belongs to a retailer rather than an individual
A note inside the package asks you to scan a QR code to identify the sender or to process a return
You later find online reviews posted under your name for products you never bought
realExamples: The FTC issued an August 2026 consumer alert describing scammers sending unordered gift packages with QR codes reading "scan to find out who sent it" that lead to phishing sites stealing credit card numbers, usernames, or passwords

An Arizona couple featured in a 2026 news report received multiple packages addressed to fake names at their address, which they traced back to a brushing scam used to generate fraudulent tracking numbers and reviews

The U.S. Postal Inspection Service describes brushing senders as typically international third-party sellers who found the recipient's address online and ship items with no return address or a retailer's address instead

triage.reasoning: This is fundamentally the FTC-described 'brushing scam' (fake reviews via unsolicited packages) with an added QR-code phishing element; the QR-code phishing piece already exists as its own database entry (QR Code Scam), and the underlying unsolicited-package/fake-review mechanic is not represented elsewhere but overlaps heavily with existing categories rather than being wholly novel. Given the strong conceptual overlap with QR Code Scam and general delivery/phishing patterns, this reads more as a hybrid/variant than a fully new standalone pattern.
